author: Unknown
title: How Unions Can Reverse Privatization of Medicaid and Why It Matters
content:
The following was adapted from a March 2026 speech that Rose Roach, National Coordinator for the Labor Campaign for Single Payer, gave to the Minnesota AFL-CIO.




In July 2025, President Trump signed HR1 into law, inflicting a trillion dollars of federal cuts on our nation’s lifesaving state-based Medicaid programs. Meanwhile, Congress allowed the tax credits available for people enrolled in Affordable Care Act (ACA) insurance exchanges to expire. 




These cuts impact all of us, even those with union-negotiated health care plans. That’s because when emergency rooms and hospitals have more uninsured patients, they provide more uncompensated care. To cover that loss, providers increase prices, and insurance companies in turn increase premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who are still insured. 




Union members who are insured through their employers are already seeing their exorbitant health insurance premiums rise to some of the highest levels we’ve seen in more than two decades. Meanwhile, Medicare Advantage plans (privatized, for-profit insurance) serving retirees are closing shop or increasing premiums while cutting benefits. Those on a Medicare supplemental or Medigap plan are seeing hefty premium increases as well.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: German Amazon Workers Organize To Get Paid for Every Minute
content:
Amazon workers at four delivery and sorting warehouses in Germany are organizing to make every minute count. They’re demanding that Amazon pay them for every minute of work, saying in a petition that the company is stealing their time.




Working even 10 unpaid minutes a day, the workers say, adds up to 4.5 workdays per year of free labor, or about $712 U.S. (618 euros) in stolen wages. And at the most extreme, stolen time can reach up to 45 minutes per day.




The petition identifies three ways Amazon is stealing workers’ time:




1) Threshold time, where if a worker clocks in up to 15 minutes early for a shift or clocks out up to 15 minutes late, the company rounds back down to the scheduled time


2) Changing times to put on safety gear and boots


3) Walking time to pick up and return equipment




Stella de Palma, a delivery worker at a warehouse near Berlin, said workers normally change before clocking in. “Some shifts are only allowed to clock in or out at certain time clocks, which means we have to walk all the way across the shop floor first,” de Palma said. 




She doesn’t think it makes sense, especially during peak night shifts from 11:10 p.m. to 9:30 a.m. “We’re already working near the locker rooms, where there are also time clocks.” What ends up happening is that they have to walk a long distance across the shop floor to clock in and then back to the locker r

title: Trabajadores de VW en México podrían declararse en huelga en Octubre.
content:

author: Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Mexican VW Workers Weigh Strike as Company Cuts Jobs Globally
content:
Mexican Volkswagen workers could soon be on strike if their salary demands are not met. The 6,500 workers build the Jetta, Tiguan, and Taos at the company’s Puebla plant, the largest Volkswagen facility outside of Germany. Their union, SITIAVW, is one of Mexico’s most storied independent unions, and is in the midst of an annual wage reopener at the plant.




On September 11, workers overwhelmingly voted down the company’s offer of a 10 percent combined increase to wages and benefits. (The union had been pushing for a 17 percent increase earlier in negotiations.) Days before the tentative agreement was put to a vote, Volkswagen cut one of three shifts in a segment of the plant that produces the Jetta and the Tiguan. Approximately 

800 workers

 lost their jobs, 

El Financiero 

reported. 




Within days of the firings, the union 

announced

 that 611 of the workers—those who did not sign voluntary separation agreements—would be eligible for reinstatement when Volkswagen begins production of its Golf compact car at the Puebla facility next April. But the damage was done: 5,925 of the company’s 6,440 eligible voters participated in the ratification vote: of them, 

73 percent voted to reject the offer

, in what SITIAVW advisor Willebaldo Gómez Zuppa characterized as an expression of anger at the firings. The deal would have also 

pushed the next wage reopener

 to 18 months

author: Paul Prescod
title: Philadelphia Orchestra Musicians Protect Their Hearing and Their Craft
content:
Philadelphia Orchestra musicians have won first-in-the-nation protections against hearing loss. The groundbreaking provisions, which could serve as a model for other orchestras, are part of a contract just ratified by Musicians (AFM) Local 77-274.




They also secured a raise of almost 13 percent over three years, which will help keep pace with inflation and attract high-quality artists. But for the musicians, the most important gains related to their working conditions and artistic integrity.




The orchestra usually performs classical music without amplification, but sometimes plays in a supporting role to pop artists who use large sound systems. During one such performance last year, the musicians were seated right next to unbearably loud speakers, with no way to address the situation.




“Our phones were blowing up about it afterwards, and we knew this had to be a priority,” said Local 77-274 Vice President Marjorie Goldberg.




STOP THE CONCERT




The issue goes beyond discomfort. Hearing loss can impact a musician’s career, especially one who performs very precise classical music in an ensemble.




Under the new contract, decibel meters will be placed onstage during rehearsals and performances. If the sound levels get too high for too long, musicians can remove themselves or even stop the concert.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: AutoZone Workers Are Trying to Form the Company’s First-Ever Union
content:
When workers file for a union election, it’s like a Bat-Signal goes off: a column of light cuts through the night sky, summoning not Bruce Wayne but a swarm of anti-union managers and consultants who reap tens of thousands of dollars from sowing fear and doubt.




A new calculator from workers’ rights watchdog LaborLab 

estimates

 that the parts retailer AutoZone has paid $210,696 to managers and lawyers to crush a union drive by 11 workers in one store in White Plains, New York. The workers went public in July with their drive to join United Auto Workers Local 259.




“It’s like hitting a fly with a mallet,” said Michael DiGuiseppe, vice president of Local 259. “At the first whiff of a union, they had their corporate executives in the store the next day. They’ve been camped out at a hotel around the corner since, and it’s been going on for two months.”




Managers have been pulling workers into meetings for antiunion propaganda and closely surveilling them to assess union support and chill the organizing. “They’ve had more corporate executive union-busters in the store than workers,” said DiGiuseppe.




The Economic Policy Institute estimates that U.S. employers 

spend

 $1.7 billion annually on union-busting consultants and law firms.

author: Dan DiMaggio
title: Video Game Workers Win First Contract at Microsoft-Owned Blizzard
content:
Workers who make some of the world’s most popular video games, including World of Warcraft and Diablo, won their first union contracts in early September, in an important step forward for organizing in the tech industry.




The 1,900 workers are employed by Blizzard, which was acquired by Microsoft in 2023 in the largest deal ever in the video game industry. 




Their new Communications Workers (CWA) contracts include recall rights and guaranteed severance packages for laid-off workers—significant wins, since tech and video game workers have seen waves of layoffs in the last few years.




Workers on various Activision Blizzard teams have voted to join CWA since 2022. It started with quality assurance testers at Raven Software—when Raven abruptly laid off a dozen testers in December 2021, they went on strike and launched a union drive.




Soon after the Raven workers voted the union in, 

Microsoft signed a neutrality agreement with CWA

, pledging to remain neutral in organizing campaigns and to allow workers and union representatives to communicate openly. In exchange, the union agreed to support the software giant’s purchase of Activision Blizzard, which was facing antitrust scrutiny.

author: Lee Abbott
title: Fourteen Hundred Solar Manufacturing Workers Join the Steelworkers
content:
Workers at a Corning solar manufacturing plant in Michigan voted September 1 to join the Steelworkers (USW). 




The vote was a close 520 to 512, following an intense anti-union campaign by the company.




Nakisha West, a wirecutter, voted yes for “fairness and accountability.” She and her co-workers use scorching heat and precision-cutting tools to turn polysilicon crystals, or boules, into slim squares, known as wafers, for solar panels.




“It’s a very dirty job, but somebody’s gotta do it,” she said. 




It’s been more than a decade since that “somebody” was a worker in the U.S.; nearly all the world’s wafers are produced in China. But in January 2025, Corning received $325 million from the federal government to build a solar plant across the street from its semiconductor plant in Hemlock, Michigan, which employs more than 1,000 more workers.




The Hemlock Semiconductor plant is one of only two plants in the U.S. that produce the solar-grade polysilicon. Because it produces this material domestically, Corning is insulated from the effects of the 15 percent tariffs that the Trump administration imposed in August on imported products made with polysilicon.

author: Kari Thompson
title: Canadian Walmart Workers Make History: A Union Contract
content:
Eight hundred workers at a Walmart distribution center in Mississauga, Ontario, succeeded where others have not: they are now working under a two-year contract with North America’s largest logistics giant.




The landmark collective bargaining agreement went into effect on July 1, nearly two years after workers 

won union representation

, joining Unifor Local 252, motivated by low wages and unsafe working conditions.




As punishment two years ago, Walmart 

bumped

 the pay of every logistics worker in Canada—except those who unionized. This was an effective maneuver to halt further union drives.




“Walmart gave all the wage increases to all the non-union folks, and everything fell apart,” said Angela Drew Kimelman, a Unifor organizer who worked on organizing campaigns at multiple warehouses, including one in Cornwall, near Montreal.




But now, the new contract prevents Walmart from raising wages at other warehouses without doing the same at this one. The unionized workers have received a matching raise, and back pay for the months when other warehouse workers received raises that they didn’t.




Unifor has restarted its organizing efforts at other Ontario warehouses.




‘QUITE THE EYE-OPENER’




In past union drives, Walmart has closed facilities rather than deal with a union. So far, no such threat has emerged for this warehouse.

author: Unknown
title: Stewards Corner: How We Won Our Co-Worker Her Rightful Promotion
content:
Workers at Hunger Mountain Co-op, a consumer-owned grocery store in Montpelier, Vermont, won a five-month fight to enforce seniority, beat back bias, and win a promotion for a beloved co-worker. We did it not just by filing a grievance, but also by mobilizing union members and the public.




The fight began last December when Genesis Van Dyke applied for a production cook position in the prepared foods department. Van Dyke had been working at the co-op full-time for seven years, was fully qualified and valued by her co-workers—and was the only applicant for the job.




But members of our union, United Electrical Workers Local 255, sensed that management was likely to deny her the position, because she had been passed over before and because management seemed biased against her. 




So we began organizing even before the denial happened. Union officers, stewards, and activists in the department asked the manager about the position. Co-workers filled an “appreciations” white board in the break room with messages supporting Genesis.




EARS TO THE GROUND




Sure enough, management denied Genesis the promotion, in blatant violation of our contract, which mandates seniority-based internal hiring.

author: Jenny Brown
title: ‘Don’t Privatize Airport Security’ Say Screeners and Flight Attendants on 9/11 Anniversary
content:
Union flight attendants are mourning lost co-workers on the 25-year anniversary of the September 11 attacks. In Chicago today, they’re joining with Transportation Security Officers to defend airport security gains made in the last quarter-century.




“I was there. I lost my friends,” said Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants. “Our union made a sacred promise to ensure that such a tragedy is never repeated.” She described the Trump administration’s attempts to privatize airport security as a danger to the public as well as the 55,000 members of her union.




At the time of the September 11 attacks, airport security relied on a patchwork of private contractors, “driven by corporate bottom lines and cost-cutting,” Nelson 

wrote

 in a July letter to Congress.




“We don’t have to theorize about what that may look like because we have been through this before and witnessed the devastating and deadly consequences,” said Government Employees (AFGE) President Everett Kelley on July 21, after a new privatization scheme, TSA Gold+, was revealed.




With the creation of TSA in 2001, all workers became direct employees of the federal government, with uniform standards across airports. The workers unionized in 2011, becoming members of AFGE Council 100, which now represents 47,000.
